title: China's crackdown pushes wealthy to gold, lifting Hong Kong jewellery sales
article:
(Nov 5): Hong Kong’s jewellery and watch sales have surged to their highest level since 2019 despite China’s broader luxury slowdown, as the rich turn to gold and gemstones to preserve wealth amid Beijing’s tightening grip over their offshore investments.

Sales of jewellery, watches, clocks and valuable gifts jumped 22% year-on-year to HK$45.8 billion (US$5.8 billion or $7.5 billion) in the first nine months, far outpacing overall retail growth, according to latest government data. The sector accounted for about 15% of Hong Kong’s total retail sales.

Hong Kong jewellery sales maintained double-digit growth in the latest quarter even as luxury spending plunged over 10% in mainland China, as Beijing intensified its tax scrutiny of wealthy residents’ overseas assets. That’s helped soften the blow for global giants from Hermès International SCA to Cie Financiere Richemont SA, which generate substantial sales from the Asia-Pacific region.

The shopping spree in Hong Kong underscores how Chinese consumers are now prioritising wealth preservation over growth. Gold and precious stones have emerged as rare safe havens, as Beijing’s crackdown on capital outflows has made it harder for mainland residents to use traditional channels to invest and park wealth overseas, while physical gold is widely viewed as a reliable store of value and is less vulnerable to regulatory shifts.

Meanwhile, a strong yuan and Hong Kong’s tax-free status have added to the city’s appeal to Chinese shoppers, contributing to a strong tourism recovery.

Adding to the pressure, last year’s AI-driven stock market rally has soured, while a protracted property downturn continues to trap a large share of household savings.

See also: China boosts market defence with National Team, buybacks

“People have a surging interest in pursuing certainties, as they are concerned about the recent tax policy changes,” said Manna Wang, an insurance sales agent in Hong Kong. “They want to be 100% sure that their wealth won’t change drastically in the future. High returns are no longer the priority.”

Over the past several months, authorities in Beijing have restricted mainland firms from listing in Hong Kong, tightened controls on offshore stock trading and ramped up scrutiny of foreign trusts and insurance products.

See also: China plans broad AI guardrails after global security lapses

While Wang’s mainland Chinese clients used to consult her on high-return insurance policies, they are now asking her to take them shopping for gold jewellery. They are also switching to fixed-income insurance products that come with lower returns but carry fewer tax obligations, Wang said.

Wang’s clients spent as much as US$15,000 per person buying gold from jewellers including China’s Laopu Gold Co — one of their favourite destinations, she said. The main draw is a strong yuan, making exchange rates more favourable, as well as Hong Kong’s tax-free status, Wang said. As a result, jewellery prices in the city could be more than 5% lower than in the mainland, she added.

Jewellery has become a bright spot for global luxury brands, while sales of clothes and handbags disappointed due to sluggish demand in China. LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE reported an 8% organic growth in the sector in the first nine months, the fastest among all divisions. At Kering SA, jewellery sales jumped 17% during the same period, compared with a 2% decline in fashion and leather goods.

Part of the reason for the surge in jewellery sales is the rise in gold prices, which climbed to a record high earlier this year. That rally has boosted the value of gold jewellery, said Alexis Bonhomme, the chief executive officer of luxury consultancy Trinity Asia.

Sales growth in Hong Kong has remained strong even as gold prices have retreated in recent months, indicating demand is resilient.

A sustained tourism rebound is helping drive the retail surge. Visitor arrivals rose 12% in the first nine months with the majority from mainland China. That’s returned to 87% of the level in 2018 before the city became battered by years of political turmoil and Covid closure, marking the strongest post-pandemic recovery yet.

The tourism and retail boom have also sparked a wave of expansions among Chinese and global brands. Luxury Swiss watchmaker Audemars Piguet is set to open one of its largest Asian flagship stores and a separate experience-driven space in Hong Kong’s Central business district. Italian goldsmith FOPE debuted its first boutique in Greater China in core shopping district Tsim Sha Tsui last month.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

LVMH’s Tiffany & Co opened its latest boutique in tourist hotspot Causeway Bay in May, featuring its signature cafe. Richemont’s Van Cleef & Arpels relaunched its flagship in Central in June after an expansion and upgrade, while Laopu further expanded its network in the city.

“High jewellery and gold offer reassurance and longevity,” said Bonhomme of Trinity Asia. “Wealthy clients are prioritising items with intrinsic, lasting value. They are pulling back on seasonal fashion at home, but when they travel, they are comfortable allocating serious budget to high jewellery and gold as tangible assets.”

title: Toyota soars most since 1987 on higher profit outlook, buybacks
article:
(Nov 5): Toyota Motor Corp shares climbed the most in nearly four decades after the automaker, emboldened by strong demand for its hybrid vehicles, raised annual profit forecast and stepped up shareholder returns.

The world’s largest carmaker raised its operating income forecast by 15% to ¥3.9 trillion for the fiscal year ending March 2027, it said on Thursday. For the three months ended September, earnings rose 34% to a higher-than-estimated ¥1.1 trillion, the first gain in six quarters.

Coupled with an expansion of its buyback programme, the bullish outlook helped ease concerns about slumping demand in China, the war in Iran and US tariffs.

Toyota jumped more than 16% in Tokyo, the biggest gain since 1987. The stock had already been up ahead of earnings on investor optimism that President Donald Trump’s tariffs could be eased after Democrats swept the midterm elections. But the strong results supercharged the gains.

Toyota’s financial resilience is remarkable given all the headwinds it faces, said Bloomberg Intelligence senior auto analyst Tatsuo Yoshida. “Compared with other Japanese automakers, Toyota has relatively few obvious weaknesses,” he said.

Toyota expanded its buyback programme to as much as ¥1.3 trillion in stock, and the carmaker is allocating as much as ¥14 trillion for shareholder returns over the next five years.

See also: BOJ signals low hopes for consumer spending as population falls

Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Co, Aioi Nissay Dowa Insurance Co, Tokio Marine & Nichido Fire Insurance Co and Sompo Japan Insurance Inc have agreed to tender their shares.

Cost reductions helped reduce the effects of rising material costs and the prolonged conflict in the Middle East, said chief accounting officer Takanori Azuma.

Still, “competition from Chinese automakers remains a major challenge, not only in China but increasingly in overseas markets as well,” BI’s Yoshida said.

See also: Blackstone said to plan JPY300 bil central Tokyo office sale

The Toyota group’s annual sales target was reduced to 10.99 million units, compared with its previous forecast for 11.18 million.

The outlook was downgraded as Toyota faces an ongoing slump in China, where foreign brands have continued to lose ground to local manufacturers led by BYD Co. The outlook for that market isn’t bright, with the Passenger Car Association estimating industry sales there to tumble 22% this year before inching up 2% in 2027.

Earlier this week, Toyota said it’s planning to debut the next generation of its popular Corolla in China. Executives have also hinted at making an all-electric variant, which would be a major pivot for the world’s best-selling car of all time.

Toyota is trying to reverse the tide by building a new factory in Shanghai, where it will produce EVs under the Lexus brand beginning in late 2027.

Production will begin in September and the goal will be to reduce development time to 18 months, chief financial officer Yoichi Miyazaki said.

Separately, the Japanese carmaker also announced a series of organisational changes on Thursday, including the creation of a new division focused on robotics.

title: Asia’s richest banker sees AI correction boosting flows to India
article:
(Nov 5): India could emerge as a beneficiary of foreign flows, if the global artificial intelligence investment boom unwinds, as investors seek markets offering more attractive valuations, Uday Kotak, Asia’s richest banker, said.

“The kind of leverage which global companies are taking to fund their AI aspiration is also leading to significant overvaluation in many cases,” the billionaire founder of Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd, said in a virtual address ahead of India’s Diwali festival. “And India, as it works down the path of building its own AI capability, will also benefit for reverse flow, should it happen.”

Indian equities have rebounded nearly 10% from this year’s lows in early October, coinciding with a selloff in global AI-linked stocks. Tech-heavy Asian markets have fallen more than 7% over the same period, highlighting India’s relative resilience.

Despite the recent reversal, local stocks are still among the worst performing in the region. The lack of meaningful AI plays, expensive valuations and surging energy prices have seen global investors pull out a record US$29 billion from Indian markets in 2026.

Kotak, whose net worth stands at US$16.5 billion, said Indian equities have held up despite geopolitical uncertainties, volatile global markets and significant foreign investor outflows, with domestic investors continuing to show confidence.

See also: German firms Mahle, Schott said to seek banks for India IPOs

India’s relative valuation position has also improved following the market correction, making stocks less expensive compared with other markets than they were six to 12 months ago, he said. The country’s higher growth potential remains a key advantage, he added.

The benchmark Nifty 50 Index trades at 17.5 times estimated 12-month forward earnings, down from 21 times at the start of the year. It still commands a sizable premium to regional peers, with the MSCI Asia Pacific Index trading at about 10 times.

For investors, Kotak advocated a medium-term approach focused on quality companies and risk management rather than short-term investment decisions.

title: DayOne secures US$237 mil loan for Hong Kong data centre
article:
(Nov 5): DayOne Data Centers has secured a HK$1.86 billion (US$237 million or $303 million) loan to help finance a project in Hong Kong, according to people familiar with the matter, adding to a slew of funding deals for the Singapore company as it seeks to expand globally.

DBS Group Holdings Ltd, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corp (OCBC) and United Overseas Bank Ltd (UOB) provided HK$300 million each, while Bank of East Asia Ltd contributed HK$955 million, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.

The five-year facility carries a margin of 152 basis points over the benchmark Hong Kong interbank offered rate, with a lower rate available if sustainability-linked targets are met, the people added.

The loan deal underscores DayOne’s efforts to push forward with artificial intelligence (AI) related projects amid global investors’ growing wariness about whether firms’ spending on AI-related infrastructure will pay off. The company also has been planning a US initial public offering, but is weighing its options, including a potential delay or size cut, as volatility around data centres increases.

Proceeds from the loan would also be used for refinancing, along with capital expansion for a Hong Kong data centre, the people said. The borrower is a special purpose vehicle, they added.

DayOne and DBS declined to comment. OCBC, BEA and UOB didn’t respond to requests for comments.

See also: Pimco CEO warns AI financing on path to become ‘too much’

Despite concerns about the sector, the AI boom is still driving a wave of debt financing, with Moody’s expecting at least US$3 trillion of data centre-related investment over the next five years. Blackstone-owned AirTrunk, for example, secured a A$4.25 billion (US$3 billion or $3.80 billion) green loan for a Sydney data centre campus, while Blue Owl Capital-owned Stack Infrastructure Inc. is seeking a A$8.6 billion facility for a project in Melbourne.

DayOne also has been in early stage talks with banks for a potential US$500 million bond offering. It closed half of a US$7 billion-equivalent loan — one of the largest AI-related borrowings in Asia earlier this year, while also obtaining a four-year $530 million to develop its first data centre in Singapore.

Once an international affiliate of Chinese data centre operator GDS Holdings Ltd, DayOne was previously known as GDS International before rebranding last year. It has brought in international investors, including SoftBank Vision Fund, Coatue Management and Ken Griffin and closed a US$4.5 billion Series C funding round in June.

See also: Goldman restricts traders and bankers from using some AI tools — Bloomberg

Apart from Indonesia, the company is operating or developing data centres in several places including Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong, Thailand and Finland, according to the company’s website.

title: Singapore, Johor and Riau Islands triangle is ‘strategic insurance’, says energy expert
article:
The executive director of the Energy Studies Institute at the National University of Singapore, Peter Govindasamy, says that the green growth triangle comprising Singapore, Johor and the Riau Islands is not only an economic initiative, but also “strategic insurance” for the future.

Govindasamy, who is also a senior public servant at the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, was speaking at the 3rd Singapore Green Dialogue convened by the Singapore Institute of International Affairs (SIIA) on Nov 3.

In a world of growing uncertainty, Govindasamy argues that resilience is the new competitive advantage. “Geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions, energy market volatility, and accelerating demands of the low-carbon economy have reminded us of a fundamental truth: efficiency without resilience is vulnerability,” he explains.

The key question is maintaining growth and remaining competitive in the face of unexpected developments, he remarks, adding that the green growth triangle offers resilience as the region navigates multiple transitions simultaneously — energy transition, digital transformation, industrial restructuring and geopolitical realignment.

“The green growth triangle offers precisely that; by combining the complementary strengths of the three jurisdictions, it creates a stronger and more adaptable digital ecosystem capable of weathering shocks in the region,” he says.

He also sees the triangle as a strategy for competitiveness, energy security and opportunity. The initiative has the potential to support renewable energy development at scale, enhance regional electricity connectivity and support broader regional initiatives such as the ASEAN Power Grid, he highlights.

See also: Indonesia’s investor troubles deepen, but opportunities remain

Offering energy diversification, the triangle embodies the principle of creating options, flexibility, and redundancy, believes Govindasamy. “In an age characterised by uncertainty, optionality is actually a strategic asset,” he argues.

Importantly, the triangle can offer what investors are looking for. He says: “Investors are asking new questions. They are no longer evaluating location based on talent, infrastructure, or market access. They are asking whether they can find reliable, affordable, secure, and low carbon electricity.”

SIIA chairman Simon Tay says that the triangle is well-poised to seize opportunities in the AI and data centre space. With Singapore a major global and regional hub for subsea telecommunications cables, Johor in the north and the Riau Islands in the south, can collaborate to serve as a regional platform for AI-related infrastructure.

See also: Simon Tay: Man of the World

Tay adds that Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia have “great potential” to harness renewables to power economic growth.

The dialogue brought together more than 110 policymakers, business leaders and experts to explore how Singapore, Johor, and the Riau Islands can leverage their complementary strengths, attract and sustain investment, deepen energy cooperation, and translate emerging opportunities into commercially viable projects.

title: US Treasury borrows record US$839 bil in single week
article:
(Nov 5): The US government borrowed a record US$839 billion ($1.07 trillion) in a single week via its sales of Treasury bills and notes — both to repay holders of maturing debt and to raise the additional capital needed to finance the federal deficit.

Auctions of bills, floating-rate notes and Treasuries due in two, five and seven years conducted from Oct 26-30 eclipsed the previous weekly record of US$795 billion, set in the same period a year ago, according to Tony Farren, the managing director of rates sales and trading at Mischler Financial Group.

The US$839 billion is the sum of the 11 auction sizes, and the majority of it went to repay holders of maturing bills. Only US$68 billion represented new borrowing by the US government, and it’s not close to record levels. Those were set in March and April 2020, when auction sizes surged to finance pandemic response measures, and weekly net new cash peaked at levels around US$350 billion.

Gross weekly debt totals vary widely depending mainly on how much debt is slated to mature. This week’s record total underscores how the accumulated debt — and the rising cost of financing it — is driving the US government towards ever-larger auction sizes.

“Nothing good is coming from Treasury gross weekly issuance at a record high,” Farren said. “The No 1 risk is that people are going to demand higher yields.”

Over the past two years, the Treasury Department has met growth in its borrowing need by increasing the size of its weekly bill auctions, while maintaining the sizes of its seven monthly auctions of notes and bonds with maturities ranging from two to 30 years.

See also: US trade deficit narrows slightly on pickup in goods exports

That will have to change eventually — or else risk bills growing as a share of the total debt, which exposes US taxpayers to rising interest rates because bills mature more frequently. Since early 2024, the Treasury’s quarterly policy statements have said it expects to keep auction sizes steady “for at least the next several quarters”. Bond market strategists expect that guidance to change when the next statement is made on Nov 4.

title: Asian rice price climbs near two-year high in inflation threat
article:
(Nov 5): A benchmark Asian rice price climbed to the highest in almost two years, threatening to accelerate food inflation as the El Niño weather pattern disrupts production of the staple grain.

Farmers across much of Asia are in the midst of harvesting the grain, and drier-than-usual weather has proven a hurdle for crops in growers like India, the world’s leading exporter. Global production is expected to decline this season for the first time in over a decade, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) forecasts.

That’s pushing prices higher, with 5% broken white rice from Thailand — another major shipper — rising to US$499 a ton as of Wednesday, the highest since December 2024, according to the Thai Rice Exporters Association. Rough rice futures in Chicago are also up more than 80% since the start of the year.

Those gains come even as prices decline for other major grains, including corn and wheat. The El Niño weather phenomenon underway is one of the most powerful on record and linked to drier conditions across much of South and Southeast Asia, where more than half the world’s rice is grown.

In Thailand, the main production risk is for the off-season crop, which relies on irrigation, the USDA’s Foreign Agricultural Service said in a recent report.

See also: China’s copper squeeze deepens as buyers scramble for spot metal

While higher wholesale prices take time to feed through to retail markets, there are already signs of rising costs in some places. Rice prices in the Philippines, the No 1 importer, jumped 21% in October versus a year earlier, according to government figures released on Thursday.

The grain is a dietary staple across swathes of Asia, Africa and the Middle East. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization also expects a drop in world output during the 2026-27 season.

title: Texas blue wave erases US$130 bil from Musk stocks
article:
(Nov 5): Elon Musk’s Texas-based empire is coming under investor scrutiny after Democrats clinched unlikely wins in his adopted state on their way to taking control of Congress.

Shares of Tesla Inc and Space Exploration Technologies Corp (SpaceX) slumped 3.3% and 3.8% respectively, after Democratic candidates prevailed in the state’s gubernatorial and Senate races, wiping out nearly US$130 billion ($166 billion) in combined market value on Wednesday. The party’s blow-out nationwide victory adds another layer of risk since Musk is a prominent Republican donor.

Ahead of the election day, market watchers warned that Democratic dominance at the polls could strengthen the party’s ability to hinder artificial intelligence (AI) development, scrutinise Musk’s conduct and impede an anticipated tie-up between Tesla and SpaceX. Winning control in Texas means Musk’s political opponents now have an easier path to obstruct his operations that bypasses a potential veto from the Oval Office.

“Texas turning blue creates a new political challenge for Musk, especially given how heavily he has invested in making the state the centre of his business empire,” said Ivan Feinseth, the chief investment officer of Tigress Financial Partners.

The broader market, as well as most of Tesla’s tech peers in the Magnificent Seven, advanced on Wednesday despite the blue wave, as investors bet that a Democrat-controlled Congress will slow the massive spending on AI that’s eating up free cash flow.

Still, both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered in the Lone Star state where governor-elect Gina Hinojosa ran partially on opposition to the unfettered expansion of data centres. The outcome of the Texas Senate race was also seen to reflect voter sentiment towards the Republican donor, as indicated in exit polls reported by CNN.

See also: US stocks rally as uncertainty around midterm outcome evaporates

Few CEOs are as closely tied to President Donald Trump and his party as Musk, the world’s richest person as of Tuesday, who has poured nearly US$450 million into GOP coffers — US$205 million to Texas races alone — and urged his 240 million X followers to vote against Democrats.

“Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” Musk joked on X, adding that “data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now”.

While relocating into the atmosphere may be years away, taking his companies to another state is a possibility. Musk moved to Texas in 2020 and brought Tesla along with him the following year amid pandemic-era clashes with California health officials, affordable housing and commuting constraints in the Bay Area, and SpaceX’s existing operations near Brownsville.

See also: US stocks inch up even as election, AI risks weigh on outlook

“I am not convinced that it will be easy from a legal perspective to simply halt his businesses,” said Andrew Rocco, a stock strategist at Zacks Investment Research. However, “if the Democrats are successful in stopping Musk’s ambitions, he will need to pivot to a new state”.

Musk and his businesses lie at the fault line of several divisive issues: Tesla and SpaceX are forging ahead in the AI race, their potential mega-merger raises regulatory questions, and access to a military version of the Starlink satellite service has become a point of tension between the US, Ukraine and Russia.

Tesla shares rallied 34% from their late-July nadir to Tuesday’s close amid investor optimism surrounding AI projects and the potential combination with SpaceX. The rocket, satellite and AI firm, which vaulted into the ranks of the world’s most valuable companies when it went public earlier this year, rakes in billions of dollars through US government contracts. The stock has largely treaded water since its June debut, holding on to a US$1.9 trillion market valuation.

David Meier, a senior investment analyst at The Motley Fool, said the risk for Musk and his company is potential near-term retributions.

Already, Musk has weighed the importance of the US political environment: a push to announce a Tesla-SpaceX deal by the first half of next year while Trump is still in office is already underway. The election result may bring that forward.

“Speeding it up is the logical response,” said Adam Sarhan, the CEO of 50 Park Investments. “A Democratic Congress seated in January raises scrutiny risk on a deal of this size.”

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Shares of Musk’s companies have proven sensitive to election results in the past. After Trump was re-elected in 2024, Tesla stock surged more than 90% over a little more than a month. The gains unwound as Musk’s relationship with Trump soured and investors grew tired with Musk’s side quest at the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge).

On Wednesday, shares of smaller, pure-play electric vehicle makers Rivian Automotive Inc. and Lucid Group Inc jumped on expectations that a Democrat-led Congress would favour environment-friendly legislation as Tesla tumbled.

Even without the political headwinds, plenty of uncertainty lingers over Musk’s companies. The Tesla-SpaceX merger remains in an exploratory phase; both companies are burning through billions of dollars on product development; and plans for robotaxis, robots, and Martian colonies all remain years away from supporting massive revenue aspirations.

“It’s not hard to think that people like Musk are going to have a rough time over the next two years,” said Matt Maley, the chief market strategist of Miller Tabak + Co.

title: China’s copper squeeze deepens as buyers scramble for spot metal
article:
(Nov 5): Copper buyers in China are scrambling for physical metal, with spot premiums soaring as supplies tighten sharply in the world’s biggest consumer.

The premium for spot copper in Shanghai jumped to 1,900 yuan (US$285) a ton over futures on Wednesday, the highest since 2021, according to data from Shanghai Metals Market. The surge is the latest sign that immediately available cathode is becoming increasingly scarce as production curbs by Chinese smelters tighten supplies.

“The persistent shortage is due to production cuts at domestic smelters and limited supplies from overseas such as Africa and Russia,” said Zhou Xiaoou, analyst at Zijin Tianfeng Futures Co. “Fabricators are buying hand to mouth.”

Copper has rallied to record levels this year as bets the Trump administration would slap tariffs on refined metal drew huge volumes to the US, squeezing markets elsewhere. The surged has eased in recent weeks, however, as concerns mount over the durability of the spending boom on data centers that has become a key driver of demand.

The squeeze is also showing up in futures, with Shanghai copper for December trading at an US$880-a-ton premium to January, the steepest backwardation since 2022. Meanwhile, the Yangshan premium for imported copper, another gauge of domestic demand, has hit all-time highs.

See also: Copper follows stock markets higher as democrats sweep congress

Copper futures edged 0.2% higher to US$14,044.50 a ton on the London Metal Exchange as of 10:16am in Singapore. Other base metals were mostly stronger, with aluminum up 1.1%. Iron ore futures rose 1.2% to US$92.75 a ton in Singapore.
